column1: # Curated root-cause notes for instances the runner cannot solve
# comparison.csv's note column by cbls_minlplib. Each row records whether the
# failure is a solver defect (with a tracking issue) or hardness of the instance
# for this method. Where a mechanism is stated it must be one the code supports;
# say so explicitly when it is not yet identified. Lines starting with '#' are ignored.

column3: Thomson problem: points on the unit sphere, Coulomb objective +inf wherever two coincide. The objective-encoding defects (#100) are fixed and are no longer the blocker; tracked now as #110. What remains is the Float jump: the .nl gives no finite variable bounds, so the box is the +/-1e9 inf-clamp, random init starts ~1e9 out, and driving each variable to 0 is a huge row improvement - which lands the search on the origin, a stationary point of every row x^2+y^2+z^2=1. The Float jump offers one undamped Newton step (x0 - residual/grad) plus lb/ub/midpoint; near the origin that step overshoots wildly and is rejected, and because a candidate was still generated the #107 escape probe is suppressed, so the variable freezes at score 0. Measured: the escape probe fires only at exactly x0=0; at x0=0.001/0.01/0.1 the score is 0 whether it is armed or not. Infeasible at violation ~1 with the objective present AND with it neutralised, so this is not objective-related. Tightening the inf-clamp to 1 makes elec25 feasible at violation 0 post-#100 (pre-#100 it was infeasible at every clamp), because clamping accidentally supplies the missing damping.
Same mechanism as elec25, at 50 points; see #110.

Requires changing x0 and the product x1*x2 together in 420.169*sqrt(x0^2+900) == x2*x0*x1. While x0=0 the product term vanishes so x1 and x2 get no gradient signal, and no single-variable jump improves; escaping needs a compound move (Novelty Jump is implemented but off by default). Tracked in #101.

Structure: rows C1-C3 are degree-7 polynomials (x-1)(x-2)(x-3)(x-5)(x-8)(x-10)(x-12)==0 restricting each integer to {1,2,3,5,8,10,12}; C0 then pins the free x3 to a bilinear function of them and four linear rows bound the combination. The search reaches a point satisfying C1-C3 (the integers sit on allowed values) but missing a linear row by ~2. The precise local-optimum mechanism is NOT yet identified: an earlier note here claimed a violation barrier between allowed integer values, which is wrong - int_jump_candidates enumerates the whole domain when that domain spans at most 256 values, and these are [1,12], so any allowed value is one jump away. Tracked in #102.
